utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar. Would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with the sound. Yes. Now it's okay. Yes. We have a late start. We earlier advised you, Mr. Mladic, to use the toilet facilities not just prior to the start of the proceedings. Today you arrived some -- anything between 30 and 40 minutes before the start of the proceedings. You waited until the very last moment. The Chamber is not willing to delay the start of the proceedings any further, so please be aware that you should use the toilet facilities well prior to the start of the proceedings. It also means that we'll not interrupt the examination of a witness by a late entry into the courtroom. So if you have not used the toilet facilities, then you'll have to wait until the first break in order to enter the courtroom. Then there was one preliminary. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it just has to do with the scheduling of the next witness, Mr. Wilson. He had some delays in his travel to The Hague, but he is here now, although his luggage has yet to arrive. The earliest the Prosecution would be able to call to testify would be tomorrow at noon. Based upon the current schedule it seems that we may finish with this witness before that. I was going to suggest to the Chamber that if the administrative hearing that's scheduled for the end of week, the Prosecution has provided the materials to the Defence and the Chamber staff, so perhaps we might be able to use that time, although I don't expect that will take much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask this: Mr. Wilson was scheduled for the Prosecution for three hours, if my recollection serves me well?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe it was as long as that, Your Honour, but I have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Three hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It used to be two hours. Yes. So my recollection serves me well. We were informed that the Defence would take six hours, which makes it nine. On average we have approximately three and a half effective time for examination for a witness, therefore, we might run out of time if we only start -- it could fit, perhaps, just in this time-frame. Nine hours is -- we're usually sitting four hours and three-quarters of an hour a day, one hour less for breaks, three breaks of 20 minutes, which brings us down to three hours and 45 minutes. For two days three hours and 45 minutes is seven and a half hours. We need a scheduled nine hours, so we should at least have one and a half hours tomorrow, and it's even a bit risky to start at such a late moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. As we've indicated for the last several months that the witness could only be here to testify on the Thursday and Friday, we've -- we've taken every step possible to move him forward into Wednesday given the time considerations that Your Honour is raising now. But now with this delay in his travel, there is a considerable amount of work to be done. It's being done this morning, but Ms. Bolton's best estimate of the earliest possible moment she could call him is noon tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I just pointed at potential problems we may face. Then Mr. Ivetic, for the present witness you'll be able to conclude today?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my plan, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would there be some time left then for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was also my plan. I'll see if I can get it going with the late start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Well, the late start, as a matter of fact, we are -- was ten minutes of Mr. Mladic's time he used elsewhere and not available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony that is that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Colonel. Yesterday we left off looking at paragraph 16 of your statement and I'd like to begin again there, so if we can have Exhibit P137 up in e-court and paragraph 16 of the same, which is I believe in the fourth page in the English and also in the B/C/S versions. And now yesterday we dealt with the issues raised with the Serbs. I'd like to now briefly deal with the issues that you report the Serbs raised with UNPROFOR, and here at paragraph 16 we see that they were a cease-fire throughout Bosnia, equivalence in humanitarian aid, and halting the Republic of Croatia military involvement in Bosnia. You confirmed for us yesterday at transcript page 3798 that the UNPROFOR BH command had information to it -- available to it evidencing the presence of troops of the Republic of Croatia on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What was your understanding at the time? Was such a presence of the Croatian Army on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in accordance with or in violation of the various United Nations Resolutions?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that the -- there were forces of the Republic of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina because it was reported to us. We did not have our own people actually on the ground at those locations, and our understanding was that this was in contravention to the -- to a Security Council Resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I want to spend some time talking about this issue relating to the Serb request for a simultaneous cease-fire throughout Bosnia. If we look at paragraph 26 of your statement, and that would be at page 7 of the -- of the exhibit in e-court, this is in relation to the first meeting between General Morillon and General Mladic, and you list four agenda items of General Morillon, and the third is to seek a cease-fire throughout Bosnia. Would you agree with me that at this point the Serbs and the UNPROFOR BH command had the same objective; that is to say, a cease-fire throughout the entire territory of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our understanding at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, generally speaking, that the side that was reluctant to enter into a general or universal cease-fire on the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the Bosnian Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Muslim side similarly to the Bosnian Serb side proclaimed the desire for -- for peace throughout the area of conflicts. There's a difference between what people proclaimed on both sides and what they actually did on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. On this issue I'd like to revisit some of your testimony from the Oric case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have 1D368 up in e-court. And I believe it should be page 2 of that document. This should be transcript page 5795 from the Oric case. And, sir, just to give you an introduction, this is your testimony from the Oric proceedings, and this is your answer to the question that had been asked on the previous page: "By this stage, had you and General Morillon had some experience in trying to facilitate and assist in the negotiation of cease-fires in Bosnia?" And what we have here at the top of the page, line 1 -- I'm sorry, it's the next page in e-court. I apologise. I must have had the wrong -- what we have here at the top of the page is your answer to this question which proceeds: "Yes, we had been trying to negotiate cease-fires since we had arrived in... Bosnia. There was a recurring theme to cease-fires, which was that the Bosnian Serb leadership wanted a cease-fire or cease-fires to cover all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in other words they wanted to consolidate their gain and consolidate what they had taken, whereas the Bosniak leadership declared that they wanted cease-fires. The reality of the way they behaved was that whenever they were under pressure militarily from the Serbs, they wanted local cease-fires, but then contrived to try and break those cease-fires and provoke the Serbs." Sir, would you agree with your prior testimony from Oric as being correct on the topic of the Bosnian Muslim position as to cease-fire agreements as witnessed by you during your deployment in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that a particular strategy or goal of the Bosnian Muslim leadership during the time period of your deployment seems to be to try and provoke responses from the Serbs to try and support their calls for a military intervention by NATO or some other outside forces on their behalf?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In that sense would you agree that the more dire or the more desperate a situation seemed, the better the argument or chances for such a military intervention on behalf of the Bosnian Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is certainly a possibility, certainly a conclusion one could reach.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And in terms of terminology, is a cease of hostilities agreement basically the same thing as a cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We considered cessation of hostilities being rather more than a cease-fire. A cease-fire was simply they stopped shooting at each other. Cessation of hostilities goes rather beyond that with many other actions to bring about a normalisation of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you, during the time period that you were the military assistant to General Morillon, that is from October 1992 to your departure in 1993, how many cease-fire agreements or cessation of hostilities agreements do you estimate that you brokered?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go back through my -- my files in order to give you an accurate answer. There were at least two or three general cease-fires across the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there were numerous what I'll call local cease-fire agreements which were brokered and none of them held.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I can perhaps refresh your recollection. I do have some of your testimony from the Perisic case at transcript 9232.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is at 1D369 in e-court and it's page 56 of that document. Fifty-six in e-court. It should be starting at line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the question that you were asked is: "Just as a general matters, can you tell the Chamber in your estimation how many cessation of hostilities/cease-fire agreements do you think you brokered during the time that you were there? "A. Many. How many? 10, 20, 30, I don't know. There were so many of them and none of them were ever adhered to. "Q. When you say none of them were ever adhered to would it be fair to say that the both parties - and by that I mean the Bosnian Serbs and the Presidency as you called it - broke those cease-fires? "A. Yes. All -- in my view all three parties, the Bosnian Muslims, the Bosnian Croats, and the Bosnian Serbs broke cease-fire agreements when it suited them." Do you recall this testimony from the Perisic case and would it refresh your recollection as to the number of cease-fire agreements and the fact that all three parties routinely broke them?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a little bit earlier, in terms of the global, as in Bosnia-Herzegovina, wide, I think there were two or three in terms of local cease-fires, there were, indeed, many, and all three parties broke them when it suited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me in whatever terms you're comfortable with, that is to say any qualifications you think are necessary, but to what degree did the Bosnian Muslim infantry forces outnumber the Bosnian Serb infantry?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My guess, this was -- I don't have accurate figures, and I'm trying to cast my mind back a long time now, which is something like 2 to 1 or 3 to 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would that take into account the Bosnian Croat forces and the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't -- I couldn't answer that accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough. Yesterday at transcript pages 3755 through 3750 -- strike that. Let's -- let's back up. At paragraphs 21 and 26 of your statement, and that would be on page -- the bottom of page 5, leading on to page -- well, 7 is 26. You provided some evidence relative to utility shortages in Sarajevo, and then yesterday at transcript page 3755 through 3757, you told us about utilities in Sarajevo, and yesterday you only talked of the Serb side. I would like to present you with some of the testimony you gave in the Galic case on this very same topic and see if we can add these details, as I didn't see them in your statement nor in what you testified to yesterday. First of all, am I correct that General Morillon and the BH command of UNPROFOR took steps with the Muslim side to try and address the issue of utilities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could call up 1D367 in e-court, and this should be the first page of that document in e-court, this will be transcript pages 10029 through 10031 from the Galic case beginning at line 12 on the first page. And here it's Judge Orie asking you about this, sir, beginning at line 12: "The last question is you have told us about one of the tasks performed was to discuss issues of restoring utilities: Gas, water supply, electricity. Could you tell us whether the parties were cooperative if it came to restoring these utilities, whether both parties behaved similarly or differently? Could you elaborate a bit more on that? "A. Utilities were something which General Morillon considered very important, and at the meetings at which utility repair was discussed, both sides were entirely cooperative. These meetings were very complex because you needed to bring to one place, at one time, both technicians who had the right knowledge and a cease-fire that was agreed by both sides, and the technicians needed to know a safe route through the minefields in order to reach the area that they needed to carry out repairs. When we looked at what happened on the ground the co-operation which we received from the Bosnian Serb authorities was generally of a high order." Now, sir, I'd like to stop here and ask you: Do you stand by your prior testimony in this prior case in Galic that the co-operation from the Bosnian Serb authorities was generally of a high order?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what was said -- what I said at that time. There is a difference between what people say in a meeting and what happens thereafter, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to continue with your answer then to this question from the Galic case. "The co-operation we received from the Bosniak local commanders varied considerably, and it was our belief that in some areas where the Presidency authorities had high control, things generally went well. But there were other areas where the local commanders were radical, and from the perspective of general discipline and obedience, were unreliable, that all sorts of tricks were used in order to prevent the repairs from taking place. "Judge Orie: I'm trying to understand this. The supplies of water, electricity, and gas, also served their own population. What was the specific reason why they would play tricks which would result in not restoring the supplies when their own population would suffer from it? Do you have any explanation about that? "A. I do have an explanation, and it is as follows: There were elements within the Bosnian leadership who believed that the only way to take back that which had been taken from them by the Bosnian Serbs, that could only happen by either international intervention in Bosnia or by the provision of arms and ammunition to Bosnia, which was not possible at that time because of the arms embargo. Those people believed that the only way to secure such international assistance was to depict the situation in Sarajevo to be so severe that the international community would be -- would be willing to intervene. Therefore, it was not in their interest to see any improvement in the situation in Sarajevo. It was not in their interest to see any -- to see the lot of the civilian population improve. To put it more -- to put it bluntly, the more suffering the better, because that played to the television cameras and would ultimately lead to the pressure that they wanted in order to achieve international intervention." Sir, do you recall this testimony of yours that you gave in the Galic case?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you still agree that it is correct and truthful as to the situation you testified about there, especially the problems from the Bosnian Muslim side, with regards to co-operation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I inquire? Is there dispute about the truthfulness and accuracy and the correctness of this testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why are we spending time on matters which are not in dispute? Agree with the Prosecution on the matter and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday they spent some considerable time presenting evidence of utilities. They presented evidence of utilities in their statement which is different than what is said here, which does not incorporate what is said here, so I have every right to present matters within the witness's knowledge and ask him whether they are far more complete than the answers that he gave yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that this is adding to what the Prosecution presented, but still not in dispute. I mean, if you say you have emphasised A, B, and C, D is important for the Defence, is there any dispute about D? If there's no dispute about D, you agree with the Prosecution that the testimony of the witness on matter D is accepted as in accordance with the truth and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then Your Honour should present -- you present the Prosecution with the opportunity to spend court time yesterday presenting to the public their side and we are limited from presenting our side which is just as relevant and is just as important to the [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you present an agreement with the Prosecution on certain facts, the public will know about it as well. And from what I understand is that here the Prosecution does not contest the accuracy. I do understand that until now it has not been easy to agree with the Defence on other matters, at least the progress made in negotiations on agreed facts was not very impressive at this moment. Now, I'm not saying who is to be blamed for that. But if there is a matter which you believe to be true and the Prosecution believes to be true, then that's obviously a matter you could agree on, present it to the Chamber, the public will see it, and we don't have to spend time on it in court. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say that were elements from within the Bosnian leadership that were looking for intervention, can you perhaps identify any of the officials or give an idea of how high up they were in the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you mean within the Bosnian Muslim leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I misspoke. I did mean the Bosnian Muslim leadership.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our understanding was that they reached very close to the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that these elements represented the majority or controlling position in the Bosnian Muslim leadership?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to be able to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. The situation that you have identified here in relation to utilities, would you agree with me that this position of the Bosnian Muslim -- of an element within the Bosnian Muslim leadership continued throughout the time period that you were assigned in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can just discuss one other point about the utilities issue. Do you recall that the transfer valve or transfer station for the natural gas was located at Mali Zvornik in Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that was correct or that is correct. I certainly recollect that there was a lot of discussion at one stage about this site, that it needed repair and that it needed a specific piece of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And one more thing. Did you have information at the time that the provider of the natural gas was actually Russia, that is to say that the -- it was not -- it was not a domestic resource of the Yugoslav republics?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our understanding was that the gas came from Russia, but the pipeline led through Serbia through Bosnian Serb territory before it ended up in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you in fact ever verify if the supply of gas had been terminated due to issues of nonpayment of amounts owed to the Russian provider of the natural gas?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of statements made to General Morillon about why the gas pressure in Sarajevo was so low most of the time. That was one of them, but General Morillon and his staff, we did not ourselves investigate anything like that. We were too busy trying to prevent the suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say a number of statements were made to you. Were any one of those statements that in fact there were 300 million US dollars owed to the Russian provider by the Sarajevo authorities for gas that had already been provided?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on to another topic. At several parts of your statement you talk about the deployment of CanBat 2 -- the Canadian battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could start at paragraph 26 of P137. That would be the seventh page in e-court, I believe, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to kinda go through with you the various parts of your statement relating with CanBat to get the whole picture because it keeps popping up and it needs to be clarified. Now, this paragraph here, 26, first off, this was raised for the first time at this meeting that General Morillon had with General Mladic on 27 October 1992. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we look at paragraph 28 on this same page, we see here that General Mladic advised that the government of the Republika Srpska would have to give an answer to this as he was not authorised, and that he would give you an answer -- their answer at the next meeting. Now, if we turn to the next page, that's paragraph 35, and we have this letter that I guess had been written to Biljana Plavsic on the same topic, what I want to know is this paragraph 35 relating to the same meeting or a different meeting where CanBat 2 was raised?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Morillon sent the letter to Biljana Plavsic separately to the meeting with General Mladic which you referred to a minute ago. General Morillon's approach was to come at the issue from as many angles as possible in order to try and secure the deployment of this Canadian battalion which was sat outside the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in the end, if I remember correctly, ended up parked by the side of the road for about five months before eventually it was permitted to come into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this an answer to the question, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Tucker, was whether what is written in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 35, but we started with the -- paragraph 26, I think. No, it was -- let me have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 28, where you said Mladic also said that all agreements made in Geneva -- no, it's that Mr. Mladic did not have the authority to agree to the deployment of CanBat 2. And then at paragraph 35, your statement says that Mladic referred to a letter that General Morillon had sent to Biljana Plavsic the same day regarding securing the deployment of CanBat. The question was whether these two things happened during the same meeting --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or whether they -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was in the same meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about what you have recorded at paragraph 59 of your statement, which is page 13 in the English and page 13 through 14 in the B/C/S. And this is your evaluation that at this second meeting where CanBat 2 was discussed, your evaluation was that by his words, General Mladic was implying that he alone had the ability to decide on CanBat 2's deployment. Can I ask you if indeed you would permit that this could also have been bravado on the part of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, General Mladic was not a person who went in for bravado without it being carefully calculated. General Mladic, our understanding was, was very concerned at that time, particularly about the attacks by Republic of Croatia forces in the Trebinje area. He also had the issue of the -- the Sava valley, and that was really worrying him, and he was trying to use that as a lever - so the deployment of CanBat 2 as a lever - to try and get General Morillon to do more about the presence of the Republic of Croatia forces and the pressure he was under both in the south and the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Indeed, if we look at paragraph 68 on the top of page 16 in e-court, you're still describing the same meeting with General Mladic, and you describe his behaviour as being bombastic. Would that not mean again that the meeting was bravado more so than actual exclamation of his authority?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness has already answered the question. Mr. Ivetic has put it to him a number of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Ivetic at this moment is pointing at the language used in the statement by the witness and is exploring the consistency and he's allowed to do so. Could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm trying to find the question in the previous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll -- if you look at paragraph 68, which deals with the same meeting with General Mladic, and I'll read the relevant part. "In comparison with Mladic's bombastic behaviour at the meeting on the 15th of November, at this meeting Mladic is back in his box." That's the language you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and what is the question about the language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether -- well, perhaps you put it to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your reference to Mladic's bombastic behaviour at the meeting on 15 November. Wouldn't you then therefore agree that the views expressed on the 15th of November were bravado or bluster on the part of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were factually, at least in our view, bombastic. What lay behind the reasons why he was behaving in that manner is, of course, a matter of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In any event, you were not aware of the normative structure of the VRS or the Republika Srpska government so as to understand the authority and jurisdiction of each?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not sure what my colleague means by "normative structure," either with respect to the VRS or the government. It seems to me to be rather vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood it to be the -- how responsibilities and powers and authority was divided between government and the top of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Constitutionally and by the legal statutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We understood that the army was under the command of the president and the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, and we knew that because that is what Dr. Karadzic and -- described to General Morillon at the -- at that first meeting which we were discussing a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you said earlier that the -- that it was factually bombastic, could you describe for us what exactly you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is standing up at a meeting where we sat at tables and talking loudly, shouting, waving his arms about, and gesticulating.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to paragraph 67 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 15 in both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here we have a meeting between General Morillon and President Radovan Karadzic, dated 20 November 1999, and again the issue of CanBat 2 is raised. And Mr. Karadzic also verifies that this is a matter to be decided in an Assembly session set for Monday. Am I correct that in all other meetings with the Bosnian Serb leadership, irrespective of who was talking, they essentially confirmed what had been originally told to you by General Mladic, that he did not have authority, that the Assembly was the body that had authority over the deployment?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was only at that one meeting with General Mladic when he made the statements that he and he alone could decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe it's at paragraph 253 of your statement where you talk about the UNMOs. Am I correct that they, too, could not be deployed except upon obtaining the approval of the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 76 of your statement, pages 17 in the English and the B/C/S, this is now a meeting of 27 November 1992 in which both Karadzic and Mladic are apologising for not -- for being unable to convince the Assembly to let CanBat 2 to deploy but offering an alternative compromise. And with respect to the alternative that was proposed, it would have accomplished the same purpose, that is, getting international eyes on the ground in Banja Luka. Am I correct? The alternative was to have a Dutch or a Belgian --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was just reading paragraph 76. Yes. That is -- that is correct. That was the alternative offer, but the Dutch and Belgian governments did not agree to that themselves, and they ended up being located near where the British Battalion was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so it was not either Mladic nor Karadzic nor the national Assembly of Republika Srpska that prevented this alternative from being put in place already as of November 1992?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They prevented the Canadian battalion being deployed. They did not prevent the -- the transport company from being deployed. The deployment of the transport company was ultimately then decided by the national governments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say national governments, we're talking about Belgium and/or Holland.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek some clarification of this part of your statement. There was an apology that the Assembly was not convinced to agree to the deployment of CanBat 2. Now, at the same time, the statement says that "but did give their agreement for..." Is that the Assembly or is that Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not know what the Assembly said because we were not present. It was Karadzic and Mladic who told us that that is what the Assembly had -- had decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they conveyed the message --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They conveyed the message to us. We never had communications direct with the -- the Serb Assembly. It was always passed to us through mostly Karadzic, sometimes Mladic, and sometimes Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the alternative, was that more or less equivalent what you were seeking with the deployment of CanBat 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The location was equivalent. The issue was that it was a combined Dutch and Belgian battalion, and I forget which one -- one of the two governments did not agree for their transport forces to be deployed in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the deployment in itself, would the government, both governments, have agreed would have been equivalent to what your plans were with CanBat 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Our concern was to have a balance between where the UNPROFOR forces were deployed. In other words, some forces to be deployed in Serb areas, some forces to be deployed in Muslim areas, some forces deployed in Croat areas, in order to have eyes on the ground and contact with local politicians, military, in order to have a balanced picture and a balanced representation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Might I say this, at the same time, now looking at the clock, I might invite you not to proceed but rather that we take a break first. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll take a break of 20 minutes and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Perhaps meanwhile, Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber of course will observe the official Tribunal's winter recess, meaning that the last sitting day this year will be the 14th of December, and we are wondering whether we should restart in view of the 7th of January. I do not know whether you have any views about what you'd like the Chamber to do as far as scheduling in the early days of January is concerned. Perhaps once the witness -- could you give it some thought and then inform the Chamber perhaps at the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. We discussed the matter, and I will let you know at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I'd like to move to another topic, and this is one that you discuss at paragraphs 136 through 147 of your statement, and for the need to refresh anyone's recollection, that's at page 32 of the same. And it's the UNHCR aid convoys and the problems with the same. And if I may say so, the general picture that you paint is one where the Serbs wanted full timings, full manifests of the load, names of drivers, serial numbers of guns, and then on the other hand you say that convoys were delayed by Serb forces checking all containers and that you considered this to be a deliberate obstruction. Is this an accurate general summary of the picture in relation to aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a general description of all aid convoys. That was a description of what was happening at a certain period of time with some aid convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps provide some specifics for us?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was around the time of January or February 1993, when General Morillon went -- or tried to get to Gorazde but was held up and prevented from -- from doing so. And there were a number of convoys, I believe was Rogatica, or near Rogatica, that they were -- they were held up, and we passed a convoy which was being searched in the way that -- that I described. In other words, every single can being opened and every single item being off-loaded and checked. Around that time - I can't recall if it was that specific convoy - but around that time there were requests for all the details that I described just then. One of the things which it may be useful to bear in mind when considering these is that the communications which the UN had in Bosnia at that time depended totally on INMARSAT communications. There were no land-lines connecting any of the UN locations or sites, unlike on the Bosnian Serb side, which had close to complete normal communications. What this meant was that to fax one page over INMARSAT cost over $50 and that was when you could get through. What I -- the reason I explained this about the difficulty -- extreme difficulty that the UN had communicating is that the -- its ability to co-ordinate the kind of detail which we were being asked to provide was utterly impossible given the communication means that we had at our hands, and the Bosnian Serbs knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You have indicated that this was one time in January or February of 1993. Could you then explain for me in paragraph 141 on page 33 of your statement your conclusion that: "In order to contain the enclaves and exacerbate the conditions in them, the Bosnian Serbs deliberately placed obstructions in the way of almost all efforts to deliver humanitarian aid to the enclaves." Are we talking about one instance? Are we talking about all of them?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about almost all of them. When the Bosnian Serb wanted to allow a convoy to get through, it got through, and there is previous testimony about the conveys that did get through. When they did not want the convoys to get through, then an entire panoply of reasons and excuses were used to prevent them from getting through. It was our belief that if they had wanted them to get through, it would have been a simple matter to -- to get them through, but that it did not suit their -- their aims to allow them to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now let me put this to you and you can tell me whether you agree with it or not, but another logical explanation for the foregoing - that is the stringent requirements of the Serbs and the delays and the examination of conveys - another logical explanation for this would be that the Serbs were fearful of the UNHCR convoys being utilised for the transport of weapons and military supplies to the Bosnian Muslim forces in the enclaves and elsewhere. Would you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly a reason, an excuse which was given to us by the Bosnian Serbs and many occasions, and I understand that on a small number of occasions that actually was found to be -- found to be correct. However, that does not provide in our view at the time anything like sufficient reason for making people starve.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, can you tell me in your view did the Bosnian Serbs have a legitimate reason to be wary of aid convoys escorted by UNPROFOR, driven by UNHCR, being used for the clandestine transport of weapons and supplies by the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They in our view had a legitimate reason to be concerned but not to stop them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that the official position of UNPROFOR was that no weapons should be allowed on aid convoys, and whenever you became aware or had suspicions that weapons might be hidden, you searched them yourselves, and if anything was found you would lodge a firm protest with the offending side?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I would seek clarification of one of the previous answers of the witness. Mr. Tucker, you said, "I understand that a small number of occasions that actually was found to be correct," about weapons being transported in aid convoys. Could you give us an idea on -- on how many occasions this happened, and also approximately about the size? Are we talking about five rifles or about 500 machine-guns? Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two specific examples that I know of and was involved with was when some explosives were hidden in -- I think it was oxygen bottles. It was gas bottles of some kind which were being transported into Sarajevo for one of the hospitals, and I forget how many, there was one or two gas bottles were found to have had explosives in them rather than gas. That was one situation. That was around, I think it was about January or February of 1993. The second incident was in the Lasva Valley in about February 1993, when a UNHCR convoy to take aid into a Bosnian Croat area we had received a tip-off that it had small arms underneath the sacks of flour, and we immediately searched the convoy and found something like 20 AK-47s and a couple thousand rounds of ammunition underneath the -- those are two specific instances that I know of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you have the details of these two instances. Are you aware of any other examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of any other examples and was not -- no other examples were reported through -- to me or to General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, when you say these are the only two examples that you are aware of, were these instances where the UNPROFOR themselves searched the vehicles and found these weapons or where the Bosnian Serbs found the weapons?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, but this is going back a long time in memory, that the explosives in the -- in the gas battles were found by the Serbs when they halted a convoy and that the small arms were found by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so then am I to understand your testimony that you believe there is only one occasion when UNPROFOR found weapons in convoys, or would you like me to refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection now, those are the only two that I can recall knowing about or having been reported. There were a number of accusations by mainly the Bosnian Serbs of the usage of UNPROFOR vehicles for transporting people around the battle-field, but I think that was mainly in the Bihac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if this was during your time, but do you also recall that there was an incident in Sarajevo where a Mr. Hakija was actually -- was actually -- Hakija Turajlic in the beginning of 1993 was being secretly transported in a UN vehicle and was found and was shot?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was moved in the daily shuttle which took the cleaners from Sarajevo to the airports, and he just joined the queue of cleaners as if he were another cleaner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you're talking of people being transported around the battle-field. What type of people are these? Some type of soldiers, civilians, and -- or what was the purpose of transporting these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The accusation from the -- or the allegation from the Bosnian Serbs was that it was soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to as I promised earlier refresh your recollection, and in doing so I'd like to turn to 1D369 and page 65 in e-court of this document, which is the transcript from the Perisic trial at T9241, lines 1 through 10. And, sir, this is your answer, and if you could read along as I read to you: "No, it was our position that no weapons should be allowed through, and we -- whenever we became aware or had suspicions that weapons might be hidden in humanitarian aid, we searched them ourselves as well. And on a number of occasions, we found weapons and made the strongest protest to whichever side was responsible for placing those weapons in the humanitarian aid. "Q. Okay. Well, as a matter of reality, the strongest protests that were made, be they to one side or the other, as we've discussed cease-fires, often fell on deaf ears; correct? "A. Like most requests for humanity in that part of the world." Does this refresh your recollection of there being actually a number of occasions when UNPROFOR itself found weapons being transported in convoys that it was -- humanitarian aid convoys that it was supposed to escort?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that we made a number of searches, but not all searches found things. The two times that I specifically recall are the two which I've described to you just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and for those two you said one was found by the Bosnian Serbs. So I'm confused by this language here where you say "on a number of occasions we found weapons."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall precisely whether the high explosives were found by the Serbs or by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If -- I would like to show you what has been marked as 1D358.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is a video, and it has -- it has transcripts in e-court in both languages, and I'm aware that the booths ought to have been provided with the same, so in accordance with the standing order I guess on videos we play it twice I presume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And transcripts have been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding that they were provided to the booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see nodding yes from at least some of the booths. Yes, could it be played twice. That's for technical reasons, Mr. Tucker, not -- first round, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be replayed, restarted with sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. One moment. Your Honours, on my end it says that the sound is turned on. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we do not hear anything. That's the only thing I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the same. Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Allow me to try ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists, if Mr. Ivetic gives us the DVD, Ms. Stewart can try to play it through our system and see if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have given DVDs to the Registry and to the Prosecution. I do have it on USB stick if that's easier. The file is VTS01_1VOV.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We have a copy now, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I do not know whether you received training as well. Your Case Manager had, but apparently he's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe this was part of the training, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But whatever is there. How much time would it take, Ms. Stewart, to play it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If it assists, I could perhaps go to further questions -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear -- now I don't see anything, although I hear a track. Can we -- no. Let's -- if you -- the help of the OTP is highly appreciated, but could you meanwhile continue, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think here we are. Could we start on from the beginning so that we play the first round.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This should be the end. If we could now go back to the beginning and play it through a second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, just for your information, in order to check the transcript, it's played twice so we'll now hear it with translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] At a check-point in Ilidza in trucks of the United Nations that had papers that they were transporting humanitarian aid for the Muslims in Hrasnica, the Serb army uncovered 24.500 bullets. Today at Ilidza a convoy was stopped that had been transporting humanitarian aid for Butmir and Hrasnica. During a routine inspection conducted by members of the military police from Ilidza, it was discovered that the containers carrying flour had a false bottom and in this enclosed space there were tin boxes. This was enough reason to doubt the regularity of the convoy. The members of the French battalion escorting the convoy were unable to tell us what was contained in the enclosed space under the containers. The convoy was stopped and representatives of UNPROFOR and UNHCR and the police were called, and in their presence an on-site investigation was performed. "The containers were removed from the trucks and then with a crane the top part of the container was separated from the platform to which it had been fixed. "Reporter: Mr. Popadic, from the on-site investigation that was performed, can you tell us what was discovered in the trucks that were transporting humanitarian aid for Hrasnica? "Mr. Popadic: In the trucks that left for Hrasnica this morning at 9.45, we discovered 12.7 millimetre ammunition, 5.000 rounds; 7.9 millimetre sniper ammunition, 19.540 rounds. These were found as you can see under false bottom underneath the container. This is the second time that in the zone of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade we find weapons, ammunitions among the humanitarian aid needed by the Muslim side. "Reporter: Were you able to see whose ammunition it is, where it is from? "Mr. Popadic: All the ammunition was manufactured in Konjic and air-lifted to the airport in Sarajevo, and after that taken by ground transport this time driven by the French forces, which escorted the detected amount of ammunition. We requested official information from the gentlemen from the UN who were in charge but we were not able to receive any, the explanation being that they were not authorised to provide information. Off the record, the UNHCR representative claimed they had nothing to do with trucks or containers and that they were only in charge of the cargo transported in the containers while anything underneath the containers was of no concern to them. The members of the French Foreign Legion apologised saying that they were only escorting the convoy. The UN police said it would investigate the incident and inform us of the results in a timely manner. Who loaded the trucks at the airport and where the ammunition was loaded remains a mystery. "Reporter: What about airport checks and how many such conveys have passed? "Mr. Popadic: We don't know. However it is an indisputable fact that UNPROFOR is unmasked for the umpteenth time transporting and distributing weapons and ammunition for Muslims under the guise of humanitarian aid."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you and my thanks to the Office of the Prosecutor for assisting me with that technical aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, where is Hrasnica located, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to show me a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that that is near the Sarajevo airport?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is this an incident that you know anything about; that is to say, do you believe it was during the time period that you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall an incident of the kind that you describe during my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, we as of yet have not been able to get a date for this recording. It was used in the Tolimir trial also without a date. We are trying to find the date for the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us this procedure that we saw here of the UN officials assisting the Bosnian Serb authorities in doing the investigation, taking photographs, et cetera, was that the standard protocol that was in place?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that I was in Bosnia, we were setting up operations. What the standard procedure was, I'm not sure when that was actually established. The UN police were brought in for a whole range of reasons. That was one of them. What the precise protocol and procedures were for doing it was not my responsibility or area of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the incidents that you have identified that you do have knowledge of weapons being transported in aid convoys, are you familiar with the investigations that the UN performed and was anyone ever disciplined or punished for the inclusion of those weapons in those convoys?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two incidents that -- that I described earlier, I know that the Muslim authorities were complained to by General Morillon. That's the gas bottles. And with the -- the Croats' weapons, I know that General Cordy-Simpson who is the Chief of Staff in Kiseljak called in I think it was Colonel Kordic into account and told him that he would no longer accept humanitarian aid from him in order to -- to pass it through and that everything would have to be searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And are you familiar with efforts on the parts of the Bosnian Muslims to dig a tunnel under the tarmac of the Sarajevo airport to use that for the transport of weapons, munitions, and personnel?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was in -- in Bosnia we heard rumours of such, but we had no hard confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Would you agree with me that under the circumstances neither the UNHCR nor UNPROFOR had the type of control over the aid convoys to ensure that no weapons were deposited as contraband and that the same could effectively be hidden from both UNHCR and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is -- that's a realistic statement of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as aid convoys to the enclaves are concerned, you at paragraph 143 of your statement, which is again P317, and it's the top of the 34th page in e-court of the English, you at that paragraph identify another explanation given to you, namely: "That the local Bosnian Serb population along the route were up in arms about something or beyond their control and would not let convoys past." Now, on this point would you agree with me that there was a lot of animosity from the Serb community, especially around Srebrenica, stemming from allegations of attacks conducted by Bosnian Muslim Commander Naser Oric and his forces from Srebrenica on Serb villages on the periphery of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a lot of animosity from all population -- parts of the population against the others for attacks carried out against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, but I believe you mentioned it later in your statement. Mr. Oric admitted to you that his forces would, on a daily basis, kill 5 to 15 Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That's what he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we -- first of all, did you accept this alternative explanation specifically for the aid convoys that were directed towards the enclaves that was given to you by the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb authorities, when they wanted to get something through, it got through. The example is the convoy to Srebrenica at the end of November, which Karadzic and Mladic wanted to get through, and it stumbled against the obstacle of local resistance of the kind you just described, and they then got it to go round or got them to accept the convoy to go through. I can't remember what the precise situation was. My point is that when they wanted a convoy to get through, they could get it around the objections of the local -- of a local village or a local element of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look here at paragraph 146 of your statement. It's on the same page near the bottom of the same. The last line of that paragraph you testify and say: "Local commanders along the route would also often make additional demands or would harass the convoys." Doesn't this seem to support the -- the complaints made to you by the Bosnian Serb authorities in relation to convoys going to the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of which complaints are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That the local population up in arms about things that were happening locally were creating problems that were beyond the control of the central Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly happened, but I restate my previous point about when the Bosnian Serb authorities wanted something to happen, then it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could then turn to paragraph 73 and 74 of your statement, page 17 in the e-court version. And I believe this is the convoy to Srebrenica that you talked about a few questions ago. And here you are reporting that Dr. Karadzic at times was flustered, General Mladic was embarrassed and angry, and they apologise for a blockage at Bajina Basta. And you go on in saying that it was your assessment that recalcitrant local Bosnian Serb commanders, probably militia, were reluctant to let the convoy past. First of all, would you agree with me that the reactions on the parts of General Mladic and Mr. Karadzic appeared to be genuine?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that -- on that occasion, yes, indeed, they did appear to be genuine. They wanted that convoy to get through because there was going to be a meeting in New York at which Karadzic was going to be attending shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you also agree that this incident lends support to the complaints made to you by the Bosnian Serb authorities that aid convoys were being held up by local authorities who were up in arms about things that were happening in their locality?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These difficulties with local populations were certainly a reality and a factor. It was also in our view sometimes when the Bosnian Serb authority did not want a convoy to get through, which was most of the time, that that excuse was then used again as the reason why the tap was being opened very slightly, but they never wanted the tap to be opened fully. They controlled the tap and they controlled the amount of aid that was allowed through, and they willingly used every possible excuse they could think of in order to justify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 32 of your statement in e-court, and it's paragraph 135 that I'd like to direct your attention to at present. Here you are talking about the discovery of a mass grave containing 50 bodies of Bosnian Serb soldiers that had been killed by the Muslim defenders of Kamenica and that General Milovanovic and Mr. Karadzic did not want to release this info to the public for fear that the local Bosnian Serb population would be creating future problems for future convoys of aid if they were aware of this information. Do you see that, sir, at paragraph 135 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I see that, and that is what -- I don't understand what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I haven't got to the question yet.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was just asking if you were able to follow thus far.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And first off can you verify that the defenders at Kamenica were Bosnian Muslims? I added that but it's not reflected in your statement.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were being attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does this show an instance where the Bosnian Serb authorities, in fact, tried to avoid inflaming local Bosnian Serb citizens in order to assist aid convoys to get through?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was indeed an instance where they -- they were trying to help. I refer back to the tap being opened very slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move to Srebrenica briefly, and if we can look at Exhibit D18 in e-court. Although this document is dated 30 July 1995 [sic], it talks about events in Srebrenica in the years prior, and it is a report of the commander of the BiH General army staff Mr. Delic. If we can turn to page 3 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S original. There is a paragraph there that begins: "Three groups transported a quantity of weapons, equipment, and communications equipment in the autumn of 1994. This method was very slow and risky, so we sought a way to re-open the air corridor which operated in the first half of 1993, when five tonnes of MTS, ten tonnes of UBS had been transported, 20 soldiers, 29 passengers evacuated, and six out of ten flights had been successful." First of all, sir, you see here the translator's note that UBS stands for weapons, ammunition, and explosives. Are you familiar that MTS is an abbreviation for materiel technical supplies, a military term in the Yugoslav military parlance?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that MTS is an abbreviation for military technical supplies, a military term for military supplies in the Yugoslav army --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. During the time period that you were in Bosnia, that is to say until the end of March 1993, were you aware of an air corridor being used by the Bosnian Muslim forces in Srebrenica to transport such items?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was from Tuzla, that airfield into the enclaves, and there was a white painted Hip helicopter -- or rather I saw one white painted Hip helicopter. There might have been more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I was waiting for the transcript to catch up. Would you agree with me that such amounts of supplies, including ten tonnes of weapons, ammunition, and explosives is a rather significant amount if accurate?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If accurate, it is a significant amount. However, it is not a significant amount in respect of the defence of an area the size of the Srebrenica pocket. You would have needed far more ammunition than that in order to be able to mount a robust defence of an area of that size.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact, Commander Naser Oric advised you that his forces were conducting daily raids to get more supplies from the Bosnian Serb forces; isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If -- if we can move along, I'd like to address a matter that is contained at paragraph 133 of your statement. Again, this is Exhibit P317, and it will be page 31 in both the B/C/S and the English. And here I believe you mentioned it briefly yesterday about a Bosniak army offensive where, at least according to President Karadzic, 1.260 Bosnian Serb civilians had been killed in a particular area since 20 January 1992. You say that you had heard some reports about this but were not able to verify the numbers. Would I be correct in concluding that this offensive was alleged to be carried out by Naser Oric's troops from within Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you refer to D18 as dated the 30th of July, 1995. Is that a slip of the tongue or is that an error in the transcript, because what I see in the document is 30 July 1996, or is there a difference between the original and the -- let me have a look at the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There's not. They both say 1996. It's either a slip of the tongue or an error and either way we need to correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, here in this paragraph you identify reports. Could you explain for us what source you had for these reports which are not mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reports were statements to us by various members of the Bosnian Serb leadership like, for example, as recorded in paragraph 133. There were also some reports in international newspapers about an offensive being carried out by the Muslims in that area, and I recall there was one particular article, I think it was in something like the Wall Street Journal, which talked about some Muslim forces having even gone across the river in -- the Drina River into Serbia proper itself. Those were the two sources. Or two types of source.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, did you have occasion to go to the exhumation of certain bodies from this incident and to interview eyewitnesses?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Morillon and myself were taken to the exhumation of some bodies which was going on as we were there on the outskirts of Kravica. We didn't actually speak with any eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that you did prepare a report on this matter but that as far as trying to collect legal evidence as to what had happened in support of any subsequent prosecutions, that was not part of your task and/or objective at that time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not part of our task, and we did not have the means or the wherewithal to do such.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of the actual number of victims, would you agree with me that such an offensive conducted by the Bosnian Muslim forces from within Srebrenica was rather significant in terms of its military -- in terms of the attack? This is a significant attack, not just a raid.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our understanding from the information available to us was that it was a fairly significant attack which needs to be placed in the context of the plans which were written by the Bosnian Serb Army in November to attack the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So are you saying, sir, that Commander Naser Oric conducted his attack based upon orders from the Bosnian Serb military in November?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Commander Naser Oric conducted this attack based on his own rationale and his own reasons and it was rather significant and not related to any Bosnian Serb military plans?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His attack was related to the fact that a conflict had started much earlier and was a reaction to that attack. Taken in and of itself, that attack was indeed locally significant. Whether Oric started that attack out of his own plans or whether he was ordered to do so from Sarajevo, I obviously do not -- do not have information about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any other UN organs ever responded to report that you presented on this topic; this is to say, the alleged massacre of Bosnian Serbs by the Muslim forces from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly reported it up to HQ UNPROFOR in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move to another area. At paragraph 299 of your statement, that's page 71 of the English, page 70 of the B/C/S. You in your second explanation state that: "Mladic was expressing frustration that the international media and international condemnations focused on the highly visible attacks by his artillery and heavy weapons, whereas the media were never present or never noticed when the Bosniaks carried out infantry attacks which he then had to defend using his heavy artillery because he did not have the infantry." Do you concede that this is a legitimate gripe on the part of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not comfortable with the word "concede" and I'm not comfortable with the word "legitimate." They should not have been fighting and they should not have been attacking civilians in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the fighting involved two sides? The Bosnian Muslims based in Sarajevo and the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but who started fighting?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, in this part of your testimony, it would appear that the Bosnian Muslims were the ones that started the fighting by -- that's at least how I understand, by them carrying out infantry attacks. Am I mistaken in your terminology?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that location at that time, you are correct. There are thousands of other events which also need to be taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can -- if I can return -- well, strike that. In fact, sir, would you agree that the Bosnian Muslim forces would often provoke attacks by the Serbs in such a manner by making infantry offensives to provoke counter-fire from the Serbs at times when they were seeking something from the international community?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And one such occasion would be what is described in paragraph 302 of your statement on page 72. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll wait for you. 302.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again we talked about it at the beginning of my examination, but did you feel that this strategy on the part of the Bosnian Muslim forces was aimed to try to obtain the military intervention of others on their behalf against the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our perception.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 3785, you were asked about - and I'd like to get more details about the incident where you describe at paragraph 303 of your statement on the same page that we have now just a little lower - the shelling conducted from the Kosevo Hospital by a group of Bosnian Muslim mortars. Am I correct, sir, that this incident occurred during a time period when there was a relative lull in the hostilities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I cannot specifically recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me recall first for you what you said yesterday at transcript page 375. The question was: "Q. Thank you, Mr. Tucker. Did you receive any information concerning the shelling or artillery fire directed against hospitals in particular? "A. Yes, I did, and in particular around the two hospitals in Sarajevo." Don't you think it would be fair and more accurate to identify that Bosnian Muslim forces staged mortar attacks from within Kosevo Hospital in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, and the reason is that I'm aware of a number of times that both hospitals were hit by artillery fire and tank fire. I know of one incident which is the one you refer to in paragraph 303.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, are we at the time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are approximately at the time for the break, and we will take the break once the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom. A break of 20 minutes, Mr. Tucker. And we will resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness is escorted into the courtroom, Mr. Stojanovic, could you briefly set out the position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We've discussed it, especially when it was announced that the Karadzic Defence has a similar request. We should adjourn on the 14th of December, before the recess, and begin on the 4th of January.
