Our suggestion would be to postpone the beginning of the recess by a week, because there is the Orthodox Christmas in order to meet our obligations and duties as Orthodox believers, and then it could be -- it could be made up for between the 12th and the 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, could you have one minute of patience. We're dealing with another matter. You'd like us to continue sitting in the first week of the recess? That, unfortunately, is not possible for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just repeat. In January, our proposal would be to make it Monday the 11th of January, after Christmas, instead of the 4th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look -- I think, Mr. Stojanovic, when I look at January of 2013, the first Monday is the 7th and the second is the 14th. So when you're talking about the 4th and the 11th as being Mondays, then that seems -- that's at least not our impression of what January looks like in 2013.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then our proposal would be to begin on Monday, the 14th of January, if I'm not mistaken, instead of the 4th of January, as the plan was originally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, originally the plan was on the 7th, I think. The 14th is Orthodox new year, and the 7th is Orthodox Christmas. I do understand that you are -- Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bearing all the aforesaid in mind, and I'll not talk about days of the week anymore to avoid confusion, our proposal would be to begin on Wednesday, the 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would then lose seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as we are concerned, Your Honour, our proposal would be to make up for these seven days, if possible, as I mentioned, from the 15th -- or, rather, 16th December until the 21st December, respecting, of course, the time of the Catholic Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, if you would have proposed this at an earlier stage, we might have considered it, but at this moment it's not possible to sit during this first week of the recess. The Chamber will consider your proposal and may come with other suggestions. At this moment, we'll now -- Mr. Tucker, we have already taken too much of your time. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, before the break you had indicated that you only believe you knew of one instance where the Bosnian Muslims had fired a mortar from Kosevo hospital. I'd like to refresh your recollection and then perhaps seek your comment regarding the testimony you gave at the Galic trial at transcript page 10023 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's at 1D366, Your Honours, in the e-court, and should be the first page of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I've given the correct page number, this should be the answer that you, sir, are giving to Judge El Mahdi on his questions. And it starts at line 3, and I begin: "It is not something that I witnessed first-hand. It is my belief and supposition from these various sources that firing by mobile Bosniak mortars from within the grounds of Kosevo hospital was something that happened a lot more than once. Whether it happened daily or once a week or that, I cannot say. The only other thing that I can say is that we, that General Morillon, tackled the head of Kosevo Hospital, asking him why do you allow this to happen? Why do you not protest to the Presidency or to the ABiH? And he denied any knowledge of that happening." Does this more accurately reflect your knowledge of the number of times that the Bosnian Muslim forces had initiated shelling from Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not. The one specific instance that we have hard evidence is the one that I've described to you. The rest were rumours and stories and things for which we did not have hard evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, I'd like to continue on with the testimony here, first of all asking the question of Judge El Mahdi: "Yes. When you say from out of the hospital, you don't mean from the hospital itself but from the surroundings of the hospital. It is not from the hospital. The shooting did not come from the hospital itself or from vehicles that may have been parked in the area of the hospital, the surrounding of the hospital? "A. Kosevo Hospital is not one single building. It is a whole complex of buildings, and between those buildings there are parking areas, grass areas. And when I say the firing was from Kosevo Hospital, I mean it was from those areas between the buildings of Kosevo Hospital. "Judge El Mahdi: Was it the only hospital in Sarajevo or were there other hospitals in Sarajevo too? "A. There were other hospitals in Sarajevo as well. "Judge El Mahdi: As far as you know, were the other hospitals also used in the same manner, that is to say, the surrounding -- that firing would come from the surrounding area of those hospitals, or was it only the case of the surrounding area of the Kosevo Hospital that firing was carried out in the other hospitals too? "A. I must answer in several steps. The first step is to say that I have no knowledge of such firing from the proximity of other hospitals in Sarajevo. Secondly, the other hospitals in Sarajevo were very different types of building. Kosevo Hospital was the only hospital which was spread out over quite a large area. The other hospitals were solid, single buildings, with a small building next to it, maybe. So they did not lend themselves to that -- to the kind of tactic. The third thing is that the head of Kosevo Hospital was known to us as a radical hard-liner and was someone who --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: " ... and was someone who we believed would have certainly supported this kind of tactic in the greater interest, as he saw it, of supporting the Bosniak cause, whereas the directors of the other hospitals were, in our view, much more medically focused and refused to have anything to do with the kind of action that the director of Kosevo Hospital, in our view, participated in." Does -- does this accurately and fairly represent your knowledge of the director of Kosevo Hospital being complicit in these attacks by Bosnian Muslim mortars from his hospital?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not our knowledge. It was our perception that given his beliefs that he might be involved in that, and we know of one incident as already described of where that did happen. Whether he was complicit in that obviously we do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And now just to finish up with the last three -- four lines, five lines of this examination from Judge El Mahdi. He asked you: "And the other hospitals, as far as you know, were they also the object of firing, or were they spared? "A. I have no specific knowledge that they were either targeted or spared. What I do know is that in reports of firing, it was always Kosevo Hospital which came up, never the other hospitals." And I'd like to ask you now here. When you're saying you have no specific knowledge of these other hospitals being either targeted or spared, does that mean that you did not have information that these hospitals were targeted by incoming artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no information obviously about what was being targeted, because we never knew where they were aimed at. All we could observe was where shells landed, and shells did land on the -- on the other hospitals as landed in many places in Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you perhaps recall the name of the director of the hospital in Kosevo whom you had suspicions was a hard-liner?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly can't remember it sat here. Whether it is in my notes, I would have to go back and look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I seek clarification of part of an answer. It was read to you as your previous testimony that you said: "What I do know is that in reports of firing, it was always Kosevo Hospital which came up, never the other hospitals." Reports of firing, were you referring to reports of fire outgoing from Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was reports of fire coming in to Kosevo Hospital from the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, a few lines further down you said: "All we could observe was where shells landed, and shells did land on the other hospitals as landed in many places in Sarajevo as well." So I'm a bit confused about your saying reports always pointed at Kosevo Hospital, and you explained that that was reports on incoming fire on hospitals, and you say that the other hospitals were fired -- were hit as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. What I mean is that when Kosevo Hospital was hit, we were informed by the -- either by somebody from the hospital or by somebody from the Presidency, that's the Bosniak Presidency, that Kosevo Hospital had been hit, whereas we didn't receive direct reports from other hospitals being hit. We only heard about other hospitals being hit through the UNMOs or through routine UN reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're drawing the attention to the fact that the hospital itself reported being hit, whereas other hospitals also being hit did not report it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, are you familiar with General Abdel-Razek who was the UNPROFOR Sector South commander from 21 August 1992 to 20 February 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In regards to questions relating to the Bosnian Muslims placing forces and/or mortars near humanitarian buildings, Mr. -- General Abdel-Razek at transcript page 3639 of these proceedings on the 5th of October, 2012, testified that he complained to Mr. Ejub Ganic about this and said: "I remember the answer from Mr. Ejub Ganic. He used to tell me, Where should we go? We are fighting close to the city. I told him, You have to go. You are creating lots of problems, and if I were on the other side I would have retaliated to any firing, to any shelling, and this is a problem." Sir, would you agree with General Abdel-Razek that retaliatory fire should have been expected from the positioning of any forces near humanitarian buildings such as the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I object to the question that Mr. Ivetic has put because I think there was rather extensive testimony on this issue, and it was also the subject matter of redirect examination in which General Abdel-Razek qualified his meaning of the term "retaliatory" or "retaliation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you can deal with that in re-examination as well and deal with it with this witness. At the same time, Mr. Ivetic, I had no opportunity yet to verify, but I take it that you have done that, that you are not in any way twisting the evidence General Abdel-Razek gave about retaliatory fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've only excluded the last sentence of that answer, which is: "I hope that I answered your question." And that's transcript page T3639. He answered again as "Regarding the PTT building --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could answer the question, if you still remember the question, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with what General Abdel-Razek said. I would, however, add that when firing in retaliation, you do not fire at an empty grid reference. You look at what it is you're firing at, and if you see that you're firing at a hospital, then that should be pause for thought for the people considering whether to fire retaliatory. But the point that Razek -- General Razek said about it causing problems, that is also of course correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you're talking about retaliatory fire, what do you mean by it? You have already said that that is not -- you do not fire at an empty grid reference. What would you then fire at if not at an empty grid reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A grid reference is always on a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I do understand, but did you intend to say that you would return fire to where the source of the fire -- of the incoming fire was, or do you -- retaliation is, of course, a rather complex term. How do you understand it when you read the answer of Mr. Abdel-Razek, and how do you use that term yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way that General Abdel-Razek describes it, I agree with his -- his statements. I would, however, add that myself as an artillery officer, I've been engaged in the planning of artillery and counter-artillery, and retaliatory fire is just that, is that you never look at -- or whenever there's incoming, you have to look at whatever it is you're firing at, and if you then look at the map and say, ah, that's a hospital, that is something that should be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If, sir, as you look at where you're firing at and you find it's a hospital and you can determine with certainty that that's where the fire came from, what do you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the training that I received in the British Army, we were not allowed to fire back, even though fire came from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So do I understand you to say that a protected institution that attacks is still protected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, am I correct that General Morillon, in complaining of this tactic of the Bosnian Muslim mortars shooting from the hospital, told Mr. Alija Izetbegovic that his forces were violating the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he did and he complained to Ejub Ganic as well. And it was not just about firing from the hospital. It was also from firing from immediately next door to his headquarters in the residency in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. At paragraph 304 of your statement, and that's page 73 in the English. It's -- sorry, Exhibit P317, and again it's page 73 in the English, page 74 in the B/C/S, and it's paragraph 304 that we'll be looking at, sir. Okay. 304 is at the top in English. Sir, in this paragraph that's now being magnified on the screen, you identify knowledge of two incidents where it is believed that the Bosnian Muslim forces fired on their own people. The second incident you mention, is this the one more commonly referred to in the media as the Markale 1 massacre?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the name Markale 1 massacre. What I know it as is the first marketplace shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If I can direct your attention to something from the Karadzic trial, and that's document 1D371 in e-court, page 89 of that document. And while we wait for that, sir, I would like to brief you on the fact that this is your testimony from the 18th of January, 2012, in those proceedings, at transcript page 23309, and it's beginning at line 12 of the same, in the middle of the page, and I will quote for you, sir: "Q. Is it true that you met in Germany with a British officer who informed you that the shell at Markale marketplace came from Muslim positions? "A. When I was back in Germany after my time in Bosnia, I met by coincidence a British Sergeant Major who was a specialist in crater analysis and artillery intelligence who had been on the investigating team looking into what I believe is referred to as the first marketplace incident, and he said to me that he believed that the first marketplace incident had been fired or had come from the Muslims." Sir, does this accurately reflect the source of your knowledge for this incident that occurred after you had left Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you be able to provide the identity of the British sergeant major, and if so, I would suggest we go into private session for privacy concerns without knowing.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall the person's name, and because I wasn't making notes, I didn't record it in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. Then we can stay in open session. At paragraphs 101 through 102 of your statement, that would be page 24 in e-court of P317, you identify or talk about the attack on the residency, that is General Morillon's headquarters and home, and you identify that the crater analysis and other information you received provided further evidence that it was a Bosnian Muslim unit or Bosniak unit that was responsible for the firing and had fired upon the residency. Am I correct that the Bosnian Muslims initially had tried to pass blame on the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you provide us any further details of what you or General Morillon did to complain to the Bosnian Muslims after it was determined that they had done -- that they had performed the attack?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Morillon complained to President Izetbegovic and to Ejub Ganic, and he made a public statement on -- at a press conference which was held at the headquarters of Sector Sarajevo at the PTT building and said that that is what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the UNPROFOR BH command consider the residency to be a legitimate target?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, at transcript page 3765 onwards, you testified about your observations about the Serb shelling at Sarajevo, and at paragraph 90 of your statement, which is, I believe, at page 21 of your statement in e-court, you talk of terrorism by artillery with the purpose to intimidate and break the will to resist. Would you agree with me that the Serb artillery had superiority over the artillery of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overwhelming superiority.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you say that the Serbs used overwhelming force by artillery when responding to attacks?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your years of service, have you ever had occasion to hear of a United States Army policy or doctrine called shock and awe or overwhelming force doctrine?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with the proposition that for overwhelming force the doctrine and concept shaping today's American force structure, the aims of this doctrine are to apply massive or overwhelming force as quickly as possible on an adversary in order to disarm, incapacitate, or render the enemy militarily impotent with as few casualties and losses to ourselves and to noncombatants as possible. The superiority of American forces technically and operationally is crucial to successful application. Would you agree that this is a fair summation of the overwhelming force doctrine as applied by NATO and the United States armed forces?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it's applicable by NATO I'm not in a position to state. I've certainly heard to it referred to by the United States. However, there's a key point there, and that is to noncombatants, and that is not, generally speaking, what we saw happen in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Isn't the concept behind overwhelming force to try and overwhelm your opponent and therefore lessen the duration of the conflict so as to lessen the amount of overall casualties to yourselves and to noncombatants?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you consider the overwhelming force doctrine as applied by the United States armed forces to be terrorism?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not for me to comment about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And yet you feel comfortable commenting about the Bosnian Serb forces. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's an objectionable question. It's argumentative, and I think the witness has already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand the question, as a matter of fact. "... you feel comfortable commenting about the Bosnian Serb forces.?" Well, the question was not whether the witness would under no circumstance comment on the US forces but whether the overwhelming force doctrine as applied by the United States armed forces to be terrorism. Now, that is a very composite question. Apart from that, it is asking for opinion. You could even consider that it's asking for expert opinion to some extent, and you know, Mr. Ivetic, the position of the Chamber is that if a witness of fact expresses any opinion, that it should be clear on the basis of what facts he does so for the Chamber to consider that testimony. Would you say that the witness commented anywhere that the Bosnian Serb forces were terrorists?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Paragraph 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 90. Let's have a look. And then perhaps explore the factual basis underlying the two. That is in respect of a certain concrete situation, isn't it? And therefore if the witness has given a general statement about the US forces, then to compare that with a specific situation which is explained to the witness, that might not be comparable, and therefore the question -- you would not comment on the US, but you do comment on the Serb forces, is under totally different circumstances. I do not mind if you want to further explore that, but please not one general statement not linked to any concrete event to where the witness expressed his views and what he would describe as terrorism by artillery in a very concrete situation. You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic. I take it that this will serve you as guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It will, Your Honour, and I think we can leave it with what has been said about this, and I will move to specific instances from his discussion in the statement to ask about specifics of other areas that I believe constitute expert knowledge, and then I should be able to conclude by the end of this session with the witness as far as my side is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, and apparently I do understand that you do not make that comparison anymore about --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the general sweeping statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I took your instruction to heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 202 of the statement at page 3 -- of P317, that would be page 47 to 48 of the same, you talk about cluster bombs as being an appalling weapon that should never be used in civilian areas. Can you confirm for me whether in fact NATO and British forces used such cluster bombs in federal Yugoslavia in 1999, including at sites near civilian locations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Then I move on. Colonel, yesterday you testified several times about Cerska, and you have mentioned it at your statement at paragraph 161 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's page 38 in the English and B/C/S for those who have e-court open.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to clarify some of the matters relating to this topic. First of all, I was a bit confused yesterday. Did you intend to imply that Cerska was an example of a widespread campaign to displace Bosnian Muslims, including the torching of homes?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on -- Cerska was on the extremity of the Cerska-Srebrenica-Zepa enclave, and it was the -- one of the early targets in an ongoing campaign, and when Cerska was captured, then the refugees who had fled to Cerska from previous ethnic cleansing in the area to the south of Zvornik and in the area to the -- towards Sarajevo, who had gathered in Cerska when Cerska was attacked, because they were inside a surrounded area, had no option but to flee towards the centre of the surrounded area, in other words, through Konjevic Polje and on towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about the torching of homes? Is it your position that homes were torched in Cerska?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I restate that I personally did not visit at Cerska. I was in Konjevic Polje at the time. It was General Morillon who went up into Cerska. General Morillon's report from Cerska was that Cerska itself had been an area where there had been fighting, but that there had not been in Cerska specifically the torching of houses, the burning of houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at paragraph 163 of your statement, you also indicate that you had heard that a large number of houses at Cerska appeared to have suffered battle damage but not many had suffered fire damage. When you say battle damage, is this the same thing you described yesterday as combat damage?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is damage due to soldiers shooting at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as you use that term or those terms, would that indicate legitimate fighting had occurred, that is to say combat, which caused this damage?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The damage in Cerska, the way that General Morillon described it, was as a result of fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, here at paragraph 161 of your statement, that's again on page 38, you say that the Bosniak commander at Tuzla told you about the alleged massacre of civilians in Cerska. I'd like to refresh your recollection with something from the Perisic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's 1D369, pages 92 to 93 in e-court, and these should be transcript pages 9268 and 9269. And I will only be interested in the short part that starts at page -- at page 9268, line 12, and goes on for the next five lines of the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when that comes up, sir, we'll see what it is that I'm talking about. And the question that was posed in this trial to you was as follows from line 12: "Q. It did indeed. In February you received some information, I believe, from among others, President Izetbegovic and Ganic, with regard to the massacre at Cerska and that massacre included relatively strong allegations with regards to people being put in houses and burned, the entire village was burned to the ground, that some 700 wounded or more, and I'm not sure about the figure -- "A. That's correct. "Q. -- were in that particular village and this needed your attention? "A. That's essentially correct. "Q. Okay. And President Izetbegovic and Ganic made arrangements with the - and I'm asking here - the war committee in Srebrenica to facilitate or at least from their standpoint your entry into Srebrenica; correct? "A. I can't confirm whether they made arrangements, with whom they made arrangements. They simply told General Morillon that they would inform the people inside the enclave that General Morillon was going to try and come into the enclave in order to see for himself what the situation was." Does this testimony of yours from the Perisic trial refresh your recollection that indeed in addition to the commander at Tuzla that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Mr. Ejub Ganic also told you about the alleged atrocities in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sequence of events was the other way around. It was initially Alija Izetbegovic and Ejub Ganic who told General Morillon. General Morillon then travelled to Tuzla, and then while he was in Tuzla, he was told in more detail by the Bosnian Muslim commander in Tuzla. Then General Morillon went into Konjevic Polje and visited Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Mr. Ganic and Mr. Izetbegovic were the source for many of the stories that were reported or heard by General Morillon and yourself relating to atrocities?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, in the same way that General Morillon listened to what was told to him by both the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you find it to be on multiple times that Mr. Ganic or Mr. Izetbegovic would advise you of alleged atrocities that turned out to be false when investigated, apart from Cerska?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly other events when the situation as described to us by one side or the other, when we actually found out the details, was different to the way it had been described to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you consider Mr. Izetbegovic on Mr. Ganic to be members of the faction within the Bosnian Muslim leadership that promoted international armed intervention on behalf of the Bosnian Muslims and against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to -- to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Do you recall complaints being made by a Mr. Akmadzic, who was the senior Croat in the Bosnian government at the end of 1992, that Mr. Izetbegovic was no longer the lawful president of Bosnia, having overstayed his tenure?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough, sir. Now, I'd like to turn to paragraph 106 of your statement, which is at page 25 of the same in e-court, and that would be P317 in e-court, and it's the same page in B/C/S, so page 25 of P317. And while we wait for that, sir, I can preface my question by telling you this is a paragraph where you give a very definite opinion on the Bosnian Serb Army having a very efficient and comprehensive communications. And 106 is in the approximate middle of the page. And so, sir, here the very definite opinion you give, would you agree with me that the only source for this particular conclusion is the limited times during meetings with yourself and General Morillon that General Mladic or one of the other officers of the VRS tried to obtain information for you via telephone?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. You are correct that in those occasions that you describe that certainly helped us form that opinion, but it was also the continuously built-up opinion of the various UNPROFOR battalions in the execution of their -- their duties, and it was their reporting and experience in the field that they believed that the Bosnian Serb Army had efficient communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you never witnessed the functioning of the communication system available to the VRS during combat situations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd have to ask you to clarify.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, no, I did not see them functioning during combat situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. At paragraphs 111 through 112 of your statement, and that's on the next page, page 26 in the English and also page 26 in the B/C/S, you provide a set of conclusions about co-ordinated concentrations of fire. Are these statements made in your capacity as a fully trained and qualified artillery officer?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself to possess an expert's skill set of knowledge on this topic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, yes, I -- yes, I did, as at that time I was a trained artillery officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you feel you are no longer possessing an expert knowledge or skill set to opine about this topic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is that almost 20 years have passed since I left the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Am I correct that you have not consulted any written works prepared by other experts on the area of structure, command and control of the VRS in rendering this testimony at these paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 230 of your statement, that's page 55 in e-court in English and page 54 in the B/C/S, you state that: "Again, the co-ordination and specialist knowledge that this required means it can only have been ordered at the highest levels of the Bosnian Serb Army." Would you agree with me that in fact you concluded that this shell at issue originated from Serbia? And if you need clarification, we can also pull up paragraph 232. Perhaps in -- this is the incident on 24 March, 1993, sir.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You state here that this incident shows that it can only have been ordered at the highest levels of the Bosnian Serb Army. And my question for you, sir, did not your expert analysis determine that this shell originated from Serbia, and that is to say outside of the area controlled by the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. I think you're mixing two things. One is the statement about the co-ordination of massed artillery fire which requires control at the highest level and authorisation for the expenditure of ammunition, transport, soldiers, et cetera; then secondly, you were asking about this incident in Srebrenica which was not a mass of artillery fire. It was a small number of shells which were fired. It is those small number of shells which were fired and which hit the football stadium and the area around it, I believe around the 24th of March. It is those shells that I believed were fired out of -- from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then again, sir, I direct you to the last sentence of paragraph 230 where you're talking about those shells, and you say: "Again, the coordination and specialist knowledge that this required means it can only have been ordered at the highest levels of the Bosnian Serb Army."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- in order to hit the -- the football field in Srebrenica and when the helicopters were trying to evacuate, you had to have people observing that situation. You had to have people who could see where the shells were landing, and that was on the Bosnian Serb territory. The shells themselves seemed to have been fired from Serbia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Your analysis of the crater at paragraphs 231 and 232, 232 is at the top of the next page in e-court, do you consider yourself to be a trained specialist or expert to render forensic ballistic evidence?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you identify if you took any photographs of the scene and the craters you examined?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no camera with me. I had about half an hour at the -- at the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How long does it traditionally take to perform this type of analysis?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the actual condition of the crater itself. If it's a crater in what they would describe as good condition, then it can be done in a few minutes. If they have to look around and find and search, it can take several hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How did you rate this crater?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly as I said, I am not a trained crater analysis expert. This one was a fairly messy one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you take any measurements?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any measuring equipment. I described that the hole -- that crater was very deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Have you authored any publications on the topic of forensic ballistic analysis or crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. At paragraphs 289 to 294 of your statement, and that's at page 69 in the English and page 68 in the B/C/S, you discuss margin of error in the use of artillery and accuracy testimony. Have you authored any publications on the topic of margin of error in use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not authored anything. However, that is part of the standard training which in the British Army artillery officers -- everybody in the artillery undergoes. There's nothing specialist about that knowledge. It is general artillery knowledge and part of standard training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me it is specialist as to other soldiers that are not trained artillery officers?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would it be specialist knowledge as opposed to the everyday citizen?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you or did you consider yourself an expert in this field?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that field, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you consult any manuals or reference materials in preparing this part of your statement? And again we're talking about paragraphs 289 through 294.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not any manuals or reference materials. As I have just said, that is -- what I describe is a standard part of artillery training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you personally draft these paragraphs yourself or were they drafted by members of the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were drafted by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Was this entire statement drafted by you, sir?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How many times prior have you testified in any capacity on the margin of error in artillery?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have conducted training of my own soldiers in that and other aspects of -- of artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was about giving testimony on that matter, Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because the answer is about -- and the relevance of how often you testify -- there were areas where I have never testified upon; still, I do know something about it. What -- I'm trying to understand the gist of your question, what it brings us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours twofold: It gives us the bases for the purported expertise of the witness and it proves my point that this is improper expert testimony that was not subjected to Rule 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I understand it. You say the witness was never called to testify on this expert matter. Is that how I have to understand what is behind your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's one aspect of it and the other aspect is, Your Honour, is that we have what is very clearly expert-like testimony that is being presented in a statement that was drafted by the witness and therefore should have been a Rule 94 bis analysis with all the protections afforded thereunder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 294 of your statement - and I apologise, I think that is page 70 in both the English and the B/C/S, although I don't have it noted for the B/C/S - you identify that the conclusions in the following paragraphs were from the intelligence and operations branches of the HQ BH command. Would it be correct to state that someone else created these conclusions and reported them to you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, yes, but not in one single -- one single document. What I have done here is assemble into one very short statement things that came up and were reported and were discussed and were analysed, as you can imagine, at multiple times during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Could you identify for us who is this intelligence and operations branch? What services are -- are --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This was the intelligence and operations branches of the HQ BH command main headquarters, which was in Kiseljak, which was under the command of the Chief of Staff of BH command General Cordy-Simpson.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are we talking military intelligence from various domestic armies, or are we talking intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean the military intelligence as in the meaning of G2 in the NATO terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From which countries?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the countries who contributed soldiers to the headquarters of UN BH commands. By memory, it would be the British, Dutch, Danish, US. There were a number of other countries who contributed but it's a matter of record to find out where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And with regard to these paragraphs that are in part based upon the work that these branches did, am I correct that you were not an eyewitness to all of the events that are recorded here?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not correct, or no you were not an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not an eyewitness to many events. These were reports which were forwarded to -- for discussion at meetings that General Morillon had and were forwarded to General Morillon in his forward headquarters in the residency in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And you do not know the bulk of the materials that were reviewed by these intelligence and operation branches in reaching the conclusions in their reports, do you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were reviewed, some of them were not. When there were major incidents or major events which led to conclusions, then, yes, those were reviewed in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm slightly in doubt what to do. You said you would finish during this session. We are approximately at the time where the session should have finished already. How much more time would you still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you testified about seeing houses and villages that were -- that were destroyed in the Banja Luka area. Am I correct that you first saw those houses in 1996 when you were redeployed as part of SFOR and not in 1992 on 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for going slightly over but I have completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm not -- you're -- as a matter of fact, you're staying well within the time-limits you indicated before -- the Defence indicated before. Could the Witness -- we take a break of another 20 minutes. Could you follow the usher, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00, but could I already inquire, Mr. Vanderpuye, how much time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm just going to take a quick look at the transcript. I don't anticipate much at all. I have written down just a question or two. I want to show him a transcript reference, but I'll take a look at it during the break. It shouldn't be long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So limited time. Then we'll find time then later on to further discuss the scheduling for early January. We take a break and we resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, first Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. I would like to take you back to a set of questions put to you by the Defence this morning in relation to the convoys and how they were checked and searched if necessary. You refer to two occasions where there were some complaints. Who was usually present during these checks on the spot and checking the convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding is that the checks were conducted either by UNPROFOR soldiers or by UN police accompanied by UNPROFOR soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you aware that sometimes representatives of the media were also present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't confirm specific -- I believe that sometimes they were, but which particular occasion, then, that obviously I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And who would invite the media to take -- to be present during these checks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The couple of occasions that I heard about it, it was arranged by UNPROFOR public communications or -- I forget what the terminology was, but the people responsible for communications with the -- with the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is UNPROFOR. And have you any knowledge about other entities who call the media to be present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know specifics, but I would imagine that media could be called by one or other of the -- the warring factions, authorities, or local -- or the media might even have just been -- been there, because the locations that such searches would have taken place were fairly limited, because there are only a few routes which were well known along which the convoys were -- were moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has a question for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you talked about combat damage to houses, and you said General Morillon determined combat damage by the fact that there were bullet holes in the walls of the buildings. My question to you is: How did he determine that that was caused by combat damage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously, we would not have been present when the shooting actually took place, and it would be conceivable that somebody could just shoot away at a building. Our supposition was that the amount of damage that would have to have been caused in order to make it look like combat, because most houses in Bosnia have got the odd hole in them, so the odd hole is simply not relevant. It is large numbers of holes, and -- and the use of high explosives. Yes, it is conceivable that somebody could have done that deliberately in order to make it look as if there had been fighting somewhere. Conceptually you are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So in fact, General Morillon's determination did not exclude this possibility that in fact it could have been done deliberately without any -- without any fighting, without any combat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is technically possible. If we're talking about Cerska specifically, when General Morillon arrived in Cerska, when he went up the narrow road that led from Konjevic Polje to Cerska, the Bosnian Muslim front line soldiers said, "You can try and go through but the Serbs will never let you." Morillon drove up the road, and when he arrived at the outskirts of Cerska, he came across a couple of Serb soldiers who were on guard. They were very surprised to see General Morillon. And when General Morillon was then introduced to the platoon commander, a quite low-level soldier, the platoon commander was also very surprised to see General Morillon. And the platoon commander was the commander of a regular army unit of the VRS, in other words, not a militia or a specialist unit, and was very professional in his conduct towards General Morillon, and gave -- and spoke quite freely to General Morillon in a way that gave General Morillon the impression that what the platoon commander was saying was entirely consistent with what he could see of the damage in -- in the area. And that we knew that there had been heavy fighting there. We knew that the refugees had fled from there, and we knew that there had been sounds reported of heavy fighting in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you know whether heavy fighting was taking place from within a house, within houses? Surely they could have been fighting on a front line somewhere, not necessarily from within houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The front line was further -- was further forward from Cerska, and as the front line was originally a number of kilometres away from Cerska, and as the Serbs attacked, they came closer and closer, and the evidence which General Morillon saw and which was consistent with the reports from the refugees was that the Muslim soldiers had been pushed back from the front line and had eventually resisted or their last stand had been in the houses themselves, hence the -- hence the damage there, and had then either been killed, captured, or had also withdrawn back to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But all what you are telling us now isn't in your statement. All we get from your statement is that the determination that this was combat damage is made solely on the basis that these were bullet holes in the buildings. That's the only evidence we have so far. Now you're giving us a little more than you gave us in your statement. I'm just -- I'm just concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- that what you are telling us now is not contained in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies if -- if that. I could have written 500 pages of -- of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not 500 pages. Five lines, five more lines would have done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question. A bit of a linguistic matter. I earlier asked you about the way in which you used the word "retaliatory fire." I'm not a native English-speaking person. I always link retaliation to some kind of retribution. Now I've heard in this Tribunal before the language of return, fire meaning that you return the fire so as to eliminate the source of fire, rather. When you are talking or when you are joining the language used by others about retaliatory fire, would that be the neutral return fire with the clear military purpose of eliminating the source of fire or would it also have an annotation of revenge or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military term is counter-battery. Retaliatory fire or the use of -- the way that we used it in UNPROFOR was in the first instance very specifically to fire back at where you were fired from, and sometimes there was also an element of punishment, of retribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when you used the language here in relation to the Kosevo Hospital where I think Mr. Abdel-Razek said that if he would be in such a position he would use retaliatory fire, would you consider this including the revenge element, or would you -- when you said, well, I understand that he says so, would you also think of revenge rather than the more neutral military term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't comment on the way General Abdel-Razek meant it. I would use it in those context with an element of the -- the revenge, the punishment aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Mr. Vanderpuye, you have more questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, just one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- Mr. President, and it does actually follow on what you've just asked the witness concerning what General Abdel-Razek said. If you bear with me one second, I will get the quote that I wanted to read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, in respect of this notion of retaliatory fire or counter-battery fire, I just wanted to let you hear what General Abdel-Razek said about that. He testified about this in the Karadzic case as well on 20 July and reaffirmed it here, and what he said was he had a conversation with General Galic about this, and he said specifically this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the source exactly, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's in the Karadzic transcript at page 5554, and in this -- the transcript of these proceedings at page 3676.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He said as follows --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you quote from 5554 in Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I always like to have an opportunity to follow it. It's not uploaded?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it public?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It was public testimony and repeated in these proceedings as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would then give me one second, please, so that we can see whether we can get it on our screens through the internet. I openly state that if nothing is uploaded in e-court, I would try to find it on -- is that quotation already in our transcript of today, Mr. Vanderpuye? If that's the case, you'll forgive me not to be able to remember all the numbers. I mean, are you quoting what has been quoted already, or are you choosing a new quote?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm quoting what's already been quoted 5th October, transcript page 3676, from the witness' prior Karadzic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that had an 1D number?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, sir. It's just in the transcript of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What General Abdel-Razek said in a conversation he had with General Galic is he said as follows: "You should not retaliate. I will accept that there are forces that are positioned in certain places, but you should be wise. You should not retaliate against areas where there are many civilians. You can retaliate somewhere else along the front, but to attack areas where there are civilians, this is a mistake. It brings major injuries, it hurts us, it hurts public opinion, because in brief there are civilians getting killed, and there are humanitarian facilities and hospitals that are getting destroyed and unable to function. So they should move away from shelling any civilian population centres." And he reaffirmed that in his testimony. Is that consistent with counter-battery fire or retaliatory fire as it was used in UNPROFOR during your -- during the period of time that you were engaged in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was not engaged in any counter-battery fire or retaliatory fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I'm asking whether it's consistent with your understanding as it was used in UNPROFOR of retaliatory fire during the time that you were engaged there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But UNPROFOR did not use counter-battery. It was only the armed forces engaged in conflict who engaged in retaliatory fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm -- maybe I can be a little bit more clear. What you said in response to Mr. President's question was that you had an understanding of what retaliatory fire was in UNPROFOR. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is what I've spoken to you or read to you about what General Abdel-Razek said consistent with what understanding?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, entirely. What General Abdel-Razek said, which you've just read out to me, is absolutely proper, correct, and should be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Have the questions by the Prosecution or the question by the Prosecution and the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, and I thank the Colonel again for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Tucker, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague. No loud talking in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I might have a moment to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand we are at the very end of the examination of this witness. If Mr. Mladic at a very low voice would like to consult with you on any matter related to perhaps further questions, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Mladic already wrote a little note.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the general would also like to thank the colonel for his testimony. That's all we have for the colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Then this concludes -- as I said before, this concludes your testimony. I continue where I said I thank you for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you both by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. Groome, about the scheduling for early January. First of all, I'd like to express that -- the regret that it is impossible in this Tribunal to grant both Christian and Orthodox people sufficient time at Christmas to celebrate. Unfortunately, it's impossible to meet the -- and to accommodate all of us, and it may be understandable that because the Tribunal is based in The Hague that the -- for staff, et cetera, that the emphasis will be on the Christmas at the 25th and the 26th of December. Now, in order to, nevertheless, accommodate to some extent, to the limited extent possible, the Chamber has on its mind not to sit on the 7th of May and the 8th of May -- January, I'm sorry. The 7th of January and the 8th of January, and then to sit in the afternoon of Wednesday, the 9th of February, and then for the -- oh, yes. I make again a similar mistake. I apologise. I'm -- yes. No, no. I'm sorry. I should focus on January and nothing else. So therefore then to sit in the afternoon of Wednesday, the 9th of January, which might enable people to come back in the morning hours and time still -- further to be considered, and then in the week after that, not to sit on the 14th and to sit on the 15th but then again starting in the afternoon. This is what we have on our mind at this moment, but before finally deciding on the matter, we would want to give an opportunity to the parties to bring to our attention whatever they deem fit to do. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the videolink, we'll further have to explore that, Mr. Groome. And would -- in that country, would the representative of the Registry still be there the day after the 15th? I'm not mentioning the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know about -- whether the Registry staff has any plans to be there. It's simply OTP staff. So again we'll have to explore that further with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's further explore that. Thank you for your observations. Mr. Stojanovic, I can imagine that it is not very satisfactory but we find ourselves also in a position where we cannot -- unfortunately we cannot meet everyone's wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We understand that, Your Honour. We would have only one request. If it could be not Wednesday but Thursday afternoon, the 10th of January, because you understand if we are coming from home, that means one whole day of transfer, which means that we would have to leave our homes, to depart on the 8th. That is why our preference would be for Thursday, the 10th. Monday is a big Orthodox holiday for all of us, the patron saint's day for most of us, and that means staying with our families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if we would then take the Wednesday off, would you then -- I don't know whether you'll travel back or not, but if we would sit on the 14th, would that cause you great problems if we would start only on Thursday, the 10th of January? So one more day in the first week, one day less in the second week?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's difficult for me to say because both of them are holidays. The decision is up to you. We would be happiest if it could be as you said on the 15th in the afternoon and that we begin on the 10th in the afternoon, but the decision is yours to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would wish that we could meet all wishes. We'll further consider the matter. But if the Chamber would not be willing to lose more than three days, would you then prefer not to sit on the 7th and the 8th and the 14th, or would you prefer not to sit on the 7th, the 8th, and the 9th, and then to sit on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is the choice, Your Honour, then we would prefer not to work on the 9th rather than the 14th. Not to work on the 9th, to begin on the 10th, and if we have to make up for that day, then to work on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider the matter and keep in mind your submissions. Mr. Groome, I think you suggested to start tomorrow morning with the -- with scheduling issues before the next witness would arrive. Do you have any further information about the arrival of the witness and -- well, the witness has arrived, but the preparation of the witness? What would be the earliest moment to start with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, my latest information has not changed. I tried to get updated information over the last break but was unable, so as far as I know it remains to be noon. We do have the matter of tendering exhibits for this past witness, and there are two other issues that I could productively raise with the Chamber. I'm not sure that it would take all the way up until noon to deal with all of these matters, but be that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit surprised that once the witness is excused that we now hear about -- the Chamber has expressed its concern about the associated exhibits and has not heard from the Prosecution any further on the matter. So I do not know what your intentions are, but certainly tendering all of the associated exhibits as you intended is not something the Chamber does expect you to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is prepared to make submissions on the exhibits that we are tendering. Mr. Vanderpuye is prepared to make that today or tomorrow morning, whatever pleases Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. First Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing, Your Honour. For the coming witness, we announced earlier six hours. Maybe it can be of assistance that talking to Mr. Petrusic, who is proofing this witness, we now hear that our new estimate would be four hours. This could perhaps be useful to take into account for all of us to know that the examination-in-chief would be shortened by two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is good to know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The cross-examination, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is good to know, Mr. Stojanovic. At the same time, we inquired yesterday with the Defence whether the six hours is still accurate and then we received the message that it was, but -- or as a matter of fact the message was that it was sufficient. Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vanderpuye -- perhaps first Mr. Groome. How much time you think you would need with the witness which will be called tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton informs me that she believes she will require between 2.5 and three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And four hours for the -- that makes seven and a half. That should fit into the days still available to us. Mr. Vanderpuye, the Chamber very much would like you to tender whatever you wish to tender at this moment, not to say that we would immediately decide on the matter, but you may submit whatever you wish in relation to the tendering of documents, associated exhibits, or non-associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think it would be helpful to note, Mr. President and Your Honours, that at least as far as I can determine from the Defence position or response to the 92 ter motion, they appear to acknowledge and at least concede that the 41 exhibits of the 58 that are associated that are on my list to tender, they appear to at least concede that these documents are discussed in detail for the most part and either are written by the witness or concern matters within his personal knowledge, and that's in paragraph 12 of the Defence response to the Prosecution motion. They take issue with -- I have seven documents in particular, one of which is -- yes. They take issue with seven -- eight documents, rather. And with respect to those eight documents, four of them concern the annex to the final report of the UN commission of experts that is referred to in the statement. These were documents that were shown to the witness in the Galic case and to which he refers in his statement. I'm prepared -- obviously I'm prepared not to tender those documents. I don't know that they are necessarily essential to a reasonable understanding of the -- of his -- of his evidence. With respect to -- I can give you the numbers in particular, but with respect to document, for example, 8424, I'm similarly disposed to remove that from the tender list as well. And with respect to document 3432, this is a document that I am not tendering in any event, nor am I tendering document 5807, which is the last of the documents that the Defence appears to object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to find 3432 on my list. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. It's shaded. It should be shaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's shaded. You did not intend to tender them anyhow, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. Would you like the numbers of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me first before we -- I have to check. You say -- let's first seek the position of the Defence on the matter. There are two issues. The one is to take issue with a specific document for specific reasons; and the second issue, and I would have to check, that is the number of associated exhibits, and I think, as a matter of fact, that the Defence did take issue with that. Could I hear from the Defence. I'm checking at this moment the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can begin answering while you're looking, Your Honours, for purpose of the time. The -- my understanding was that previously when the Defence had objected that the motions were not in compliance with the guidelines that after a while we were told that to not use that anymore as a -- as a bases, so I don't believe that in this particular instance we've objected to the large number of exhibits as being not in compliance with the guidelines. We did identify, as counsel indicated, eight instances where we had specific objections to specify documents. Counsel has dealt with all of them except for number 19264, which is at paragraph 39 of the witness's statement and for which we did have an additional objection based upon the fact that he's merely reciting a paragraph from the document into the record. The document is not offered by him and he does not identify any prior knowledge of the document or personal knowledge of the matters contained therein. So those were the specific objections that we made to the associated exhibits, and if counsel is removing the ones that he's identified, then we're only left with the specific objection to number 19264.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you'll find that on page 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- and I'm not tendering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that it's only on the specific documents that the Defence has -- has reserved its right to -- no, have complaint, and that the request to have them admitted would be denied. So you have limited your response there to that. We'll consider it and we'll finally decide on the matter tomorrow. Now at what time should we start, Mr. Groome? A brief -- if we would start with the witness not later than 12.00, how much time you think you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the matters that I wish to raise should only take about 15 minutes. I do have some recent information from the -- from Ms. Bolton, although that doesn't change the start time. The witness's bag with the clothes that he wanted to wear to court doesn't arrive in The Hague until 10.00 tomorrow, so just simply to have a time just to prepare himself to appear before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in order to lose as little time as possible, perhaps it would be good that we take half an hour in the first session at 11.00, that we then take a break of half an hour, and that we then start with the testimony of the witness starting at 12.00, which would allow sufficient time, I take it, for the matters you wish to raise, and then that we have full sessions on from 12.00, that is, one session of one hour, one session of 55 minutes, and then 20 minutes' break between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution is grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any comments on that? If not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 10th of October, at 11.00 in the morning in this same Courtroom I.
